questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to cook the perfect British sausages at home
Why fast food is becoming popular in Canada
How spices are grown and sold in west Africa
A woman saving Ghana's traditional recipes
questions.why: Rob says they'll hear about one woman's quest to preserve her country's traditional recipes.

options: Fufu made with yam and plantain
Sausages with mashed potato
Burgers and fries
A spicy Ghanaian soup
questions.why: Rob says his favourite is bangers and mash – sausage and mashed potato.

questions.q: What was Abena Offeh-Gyimah's childhood in Canada like?
options: She never ate Ghanaian food until she was an adult
She worked in her family's restaurant after school
Burgers with friends, Ghanaian food at home
She learned to cook from Canadian cookery books
questions.why: After school she'd go for burgers and fries with friends, then eat traditional Ghanaian food with her family.

questions.q: What surprised Abena when she moved back to Ghana?
options: Many traditional ingredients were no longer used
Everyone still cooked in exactly the old way
Ghanaian food was much spicier than she remembered
Nobody in the cities ate fufu any more
questions.why: Many traditional spices and ingredients were no longer used, and tomato ketchup was more common.

questions.q: How is fufu often made in Ghana today?
options: By pounding yam and plantain by hand
By buying it ready to eat in restaurants
By cooking it slowly over an open fire
From potato flour, cooked on a stove
questions.why: Abena says now you can just buy potato flour and make fufu on the stove.

questions.q: What does Abena feel is being lost with the modern way of cooking?
options: The healthy vitamins in fresh vegetables
The shared experience of cooking together
The chance to sell food at local markets
The skill of growing yams and plantains
questions.why: She says 'we're losing that… communal experience of cutting the yam and cutting the plantain and cooking it'.

questions.q: What did Abena do to help?
options: She travelled to rural areas to record dishes
She opened a cooking school in the capital city
She wrote to the government asking for new laws
She started selling traditional spices online
questions.why: She travelled across the Accra East region to document indigenous dishes.

questions.q: Why were young Ghanaians losing cooking skills?
options: Their schools stopped teaching cookery
Traditional ingredients became too expensive
Recipes were spoken, not written down
Most families moved away to Canada
questions.why: Sam says recipes were passed down orally from mother to daughter instead of being written down.
